high_level_description: Strictly non-photographic, wordless Edo ukiyo-e woodblock illustration: four equal-scale workshop specialists transform one secular river-bird design from brush drawing to carved cherry block, registered color printing and finished sheet, each person handling only the material expected by the next station in one continuous flat composition without labels or arrows.

compositional_deconstruction.background: A pale unprinted washi field holds one continuous Edo workshop tableau above a single muted-grey ground band, with flat indigo, persimmon, moss green and dense black shapes. Every figure and object uses crisp carved contours and unmodeled color. No realistic room depth, photographic light, gradient, title cartouche, signature, seal, alphabet, numeral, caption, arrow, flowchart, interface, hierarchy marker, throne or modern machine appears.

elements.desc: Low connected print-workshop bench extending diagonally through the composition, made from plain dark-brown wood at one consistent scale. Four clearly separated work surfaces hold respectively a brush stone, cherry block, pigment pads and clean paper, so each station receives a physically different material; no written instruction, numbered lane, arrow, conveyor, barrier, lock or raised supervisory platform appears.

Adult Edo-period Japanese print designer seated at upper-left, light-medium skin tone, straight black hair tied low, plain persimmon kosode, charcoal obi and white tabi. With a concentrated neutral expression, he finishes one black-ink river-bird drawing on thin washi and looks only toward that sheet; he carries no carving knife, baren, publisher seal, badge, crown or command staff.

Adult Edo-period Japanese block carver seated at center-left, light-medium skin tone, black hair under an indigo headcloth, moss-green kosode, dark-grey obi and white tabi. He studies the transferred key drawing while cutting its black contours into cherry wood with one small chisel; no printing pigments, finished edition, authority emblem, writing brush, rank marker or judging gesture appears.

Adult Edo-period Japanese printer kneeling at center-right, light-medium skin tone, short black hair, plain indigo kosode, persimmon apron and white tabi. With calm downward gaze, he rubs a round baren across washi aligned to the carved block by two corner notches; he holds no design brush, carving chisel, publisher badge, written order, crown or supervisory tool.

Adult Edo-period Japanese publisher seated at lower-right at the same scale as the other specialists, light-medium skin tone, black hair tied back, charcoal kosode, moss-green haori and white tabi. He inspects one completed river-bird print with an attentive neutral expression while keeping both hands below his chest; no throne, podium, signature stamp, money, weapon, title or oversized body appears.

Thin key-drawing sheet lying between designer and carver, carrying one original secular scene of two long-legged river birds beside reeds, drawn in clean black lines with three empty color regions. Its exact rectangular proportions match the carver's working surface; it contains no character, numeral, name, signature, cartouche, religious figure, official crest or directional mark.

Rectangular cherry printing block secured on the middle bench, bearing the same two river birds and reeds cut in reverse relief, plus two plain registration notches along adjacent edges. Its subject and proportions match the key drawing while its material is unmistakably wood; no letters, numerals, seal impression, hidden compartment, endpoint, command symbol or decorative text appears.

Finished multicolor washi print resting between printer and publisher, showing the same two river birds and reeds in exact registration with flat indigo water, persimmon wings and moss-green plants. The final sheet visibly differs in material and state from drawing and block while preserving their subject; no signature, cartouche, alphabet, numeral, approval stamp, medal or arrow appears.
